**#3224 is two bugs, not one.** `gaia init` itself exits 0 after a model fails to load — the "Models verified: 1/2 passed" path only warns. And `init --check` asks "is the model file downloaded?", never "does it load?". Fixing only `--check` still leaves a first-boot gate that passes on a broken profile, so both halves need to move together.

| Issue | Site | Shape |

Confirmed, and the report is precise — thanks for the careful separation from #2918/#3069/#2090.

The email agent picks its model from **hardware**, not from your profile. If the machine has an NPU and `gemma4-it-e2b-FLM` has ever been downloaded, the agent selects it — it never looks at the installed profile, at `default_device`/`default_model` in `~/.gaia/config.json`, or at the manifest's `models:` list. Your box satisfies both conditions, so the `email` profile's GGUF pin is simply not part of the decision.

The embedder swap and the cleared embeddings are downstream of that single choice, not a second bug: the agent switches to the NPU embedder whenever the chosen chat model is the FLM one. Fix the model selection and the embedding wipe stops with it.

Also worth noting: "pinned in Lemonade" and "loaded in Lemonade" don't influence the check at all — it only asks whether the FLM model is *downloaded*, which is why your pinned GGUF didn't win.

Escalating for the design call on precedence and on making the unverifiable case refuse — @kovtcharov-amd. Your acceptance criteria look like the right shape to me.

<details>
<summary>🔍 Technical details</summary>

**Selection point:** `hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/model_select.py:130` (`resolve_default_email_model`). It returns `NPU_EMAIL_MODEL_ID` when `_probe_npu_available()` (`/system-info` → `devices.amd_npu.available`) and `_probe_model_present()` both pass. `_probe_model_present` (`model_select.py:75`) queries `GET /models` — the **downloaded** list — so a pinned/resident GGUF model is invisible to it, matching your log. The module docstring's "already serves that model" overstates what the probe checks.

**No profile input anywhere in the chain:**
- `gaia_agent_email/agent.py:913` — `config.model_id or resolve_default_email_model(...)`. The daemon-launched sidecar leaves `model_id` unset, so the probe decides.
- `src/gaia/config.py:142` `resolve_model()` (which honours `default_model`) is only applied in the CLI at `src/gaia/cli.py:3143` for model-bearing commands — the sidecar path never calls it.
- The manifest's `models:` list (`hub/agents/email/python/gaia-agent.yaml`) is not consulted at construction time at all.

**Embedder cascade:** `agent.py:931-934` sets `embedding_model = get_embedding_model_for_device("npu")` *iff* `effective_model_id == NPU_EMAIL_MODEL_ID`, else `None`. So `embed-gemma-300m-FLM` is purely a consequence of the chat-model choice; `src/gaia/agents/base/memory.py:526` then invalidates stored vectors on the embedder delta. Note `get_embedding_model_for_device` (`src/gaia/agents/registry.py:348`) is device-keyed and would have returned the GGUF embedder for your configured `gpu` — it's the hardcoded `"npu"` argument that bypasses it.

**Context ceiling:** `npuCtxSize = 32768` in `tui/internal/ui/preflight/ctxsize.go:50` is chosen from the session's profile, which `--model` doesn't update — hence the 32K report on an overridden turn. That part overlaps #2918.

**Shape of a fix:** make the profile/manifest the highest-precedence input to `resolve_default_email_model`, with the hardware probe used only to *validate* it (and refuse when it can't be honoured), rather than to *choose*.
</details>

comments.body:
## SLM vs LLM on categorization — measured

We ran the Specific AI triage classifier head-to-head against Gemma-4-E4B on the same 307 emails. **Models only** — the heuristic rules and confidence escalation were taken out of the loop, so every email went to both models. This answers the question the issue opens with: do we have a comparison of the SLM against the LLM for the categorization it claims to provide.

| | SLM | Gemma-4-E4B |
|---|---|---|
| **Accuracy** | **70.0%** | **76.9%** |
| **Latency, median** | **0.023 s** | **13.6 s** |
| Latency, p95 | 0.035 s | 17.9 s |

The 7-point overall gap is the least interesting number here, because **the two models fail in opposite places:**

| Category | SLM | Gemma-4-E4B |
|---|---|---|
| PERSONAL | **97.0%** | 24.2% |
| NEEDS_RESPONSE | 90.0% | 95.0% |
| PROMOTIONAL | 80.8% | 79.8% |
| URGENT | 70.9% | 89.1% |
| FYI | 10.9% | **70.9%** |

The SLM is ~590× faster and far better on PERSONAL — the category our own eval baseline has flagged as the weakest axis. It is much worse on FYI. Neither model dominates.

**Two things about that comparison worth stating before anyone reads the top line as a verdict.**

The models are not the same class of thing. The SLM is a ~110M-parameter BERT classifier that emits a label; Gemma-4-E4B is a ~4B generative model that reasons in prose and then emits JSON. Scoring them against each other on aggregate accuracy and calling a 7-point difference a loss is the wrong frame — the useful reading is per category, where the SLM wins PERSONAL 97.0% to 24.2% and loses FYI 10.9% to 70.9%.

PERSONAL matters more than its share of the corpus suggests: it is the axis our own recorded eval baseline flags as the weakest (`personal_recall` 0.182, tracked in #2667). The SLM is markedly better at exactly the thing the current pipeline is worst at, and markedly worse at one the pipeline already handles.

## What integrating it would actually take

**1. Spam has to be added to the SLM before the rest is worth doing.** Today the SLM returns `{category, confidence, source}` — no spam field, on all 307 records. GAIA decides category and `is_spam` independently, and *either* unresolved sends the message to the LLM. So even when the SLM answers the category perfectly, the message still goes to the LLM for the spam verdict, and the call count doesn't drop. Adding a spam output to the SLM is the change that makes the rest pay off.

**2. The Gmail label rules would have to go.** The confident rules read Gmail's own category labels. Outlook supplies no equivalent, so Outlook users fall through to guesswork on every message. Levelling the two providers means removing those rules and relying on the SLM — which is only viable if its accuracy is acceptable on its own.

**3. Truncation is real but smaller than expected.** The SLM caps at 512 tokens. On this corpus that binds on **13 of 307 messages** (median length 150 tokens, p95 487). Worth fixing eventually; not the dominant factor today.

## How this was run

**The test.** Every one of the 307 emails was sent to both models, one at a time, with a single question: assign one of `URGENT / NEEDS_RESPONSE / FYI / PROMOTIONAL / PERSONAL`. The answer was compared against the corpus label, and the wall-clock time of the inference call was recorded. Nothing else was asked of either model, and **the rules and confidence-escalation layer were removed from the loop** — otherwise we would be measuring the pipeline rather than the models.

**The dataset** is already in this repo: [`tests/fixtures/email/vendor_corpus_seed.jsonl`](https://github.com/amd/gaia/blob/main/tests/fixtures/email/vendor_corpus_seed.jsonl) — 307 committed records, schema documented in [`tests/fixtures/email/_schema.md`](https://github.com/amd/gaia/blob/main/tests/fixtures/email/_schema.md). Distribution: 55 URGENT / 60 NEEDS_RESPONSE / 55 FYI / 104 PROMOTIONAL / 33 PERSONAL. No new data was created for this run, and the file's SHA-256 is recorded with the results so a re-run can prove it used the same bytes.

**A worked example.** One record, and what each model actually receives from it:

The source record (`0083d9aa-…`, `source_dataset: boundary_synth`):

```
sender  : James Whitmore <james.whitmore@accelertech-solutions.com>
subject : ACTION REQUIRED: Your ROCm CI cluster will lose discount tier today
body    : Hi Daniel, I noticed your team is evaluating next-gen GPU acceleration
          frameworks for the MI-series validation pipeline, and we need to act fast.
          Your ROCm CI cluster discount tier expires TODAY at 4PM PST...
          To secure this before expiration, reply to this email or click here:
          [activate-reserved-tier]                                    (795 chars)

withheld from both models — scoring side only:
  category = PROMOTIONAL   is_phishing = true   promotional_subtype = adversarial
```

**What the SLM gets — its entire input, 937 characters:**

```
From: James Whitmore <james.whitmore@accelertech-solutions.com>
Subject: ACTION REQUIRED: Your ROCm CI cluster will lose discount tier today

Hi Daniel,
I noticed your team is evaluating next-gen GPU acceleration frameworks...
```

No system prompt, no taxonomy, no examples. It has never been told what the five categories mean — that lives in its trained weights.

**What the LLM gets — 6,035 characters.** That splits into two very different things:

| | chars | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| SLM total input | 937 | the email |
| LLM user message | 1,029 | **the same email**, plus `Classify this email.` and the untrusted-body delimiters |
| LLM system prompt | 5,006 | the task definition — five categories, precedence order, disambiguation rules, worked examples |

**The email content is the same to within 92 characters of wrapper. The entire 6.4× is the system prompt — instructions, not extra email.**

That is worth being explicit about, because "you gave the LLM 6× more input" is the obvious objection and it does not survive the breakdown. Neither model was given more of the *message* to work with.

The system prompt cannot be equalised, in either direction, and that is a property of the models rather than a choice we made:

- **The SLM cannot receive one.** It is a BERT sequence classifier. Its input is the email text and its five output labels are fixed in the trained head — there is nowhere to put instructions, and it does not need them, because the taxonomy is what it was trained on.
- **Removing it from the LLM would break the test, not level it.** Gemma has never seen this taxonomy. Without the prompt it does not know the five categories exist, and would be scored on a task it was never told about.

So each model is given the task the only way it can receive it — the SLM through training, the LLM through instructions — which is also exactly how GAIA runs each of them today. Equalising the character counts would mean handicapping one model to match the other's interface, which would measure less, not more.

**This record is also a good illustration of why per-category matters.** It is adversarial marketing engineered to look urgent. The LLM's system prompt instructs it to classify a same-day deadline as URGENT, and the email says "expires TODAY" — the LLM called it `URGENT`, the SLM called it `PROMOTIONAL`, and `PROMOTIONAL` is correct. Whether that generalises across the corpus's 42 adversarial records is checkable from the per-item rows; we have not measured it, and it is not reflected in the numbers above.

**Reproducing it** is a single command against a running Lemonade with the pinned model, plus a `--limit N` smoke mode. The harness writes a per-item row for every email — id, true label, both predictions, both latencies, truncation flag — so every aggregate above can be re-derived and audited rather than taken on trust.


<details>
<summary>Method — how the numbers were produced</summary>

**Both arms, same emails, same order, labels stripped.** Ground-truth `category`, `is_phishing` and `promotional_subtype` are scoring-side only and never reach a model (asserted in code).

**Each arm receives what GAIA itself would build for it** — imported from the shipped code, not reimplemented: `format_slm_input()` for the SLM, `_SYSTEM_PROMPT` + `_build_user_prompt()` for the LLM. This asymmetry is inherent and recorded: the SLM gets no system prompt at all (its taxonomy is in trained weights), the LLM gets ~758 words of taxonomy, precedence and worked examples. Email content reaching each model is near-identical (937 vs 1,029 chars for the sample record); the whole difference is the 5,006-char system prompt.

**Truncation is applied once at the source**, using the SLM's own tokenizer, and the identical text goes to both arms — truncating each arm with its own tokenizer would give them different content and misattribute a truncation penalty to one model. The body is truncated with the header's token cost reserved, so `From:`/`Subject:` survive. 13/307 truncated.

**The agent path is bypassed entirely** — no `triage_inbox_impl`, no `pre_scan_inbox_impl`, no rules, no confidence gating.

**Determinism / pinning:** `model_id` pinned explicitly rather than auto-resolved (the resolver silently substitutes an NPU FastFlowLM variant when an NPU is present; the harness asserts the loaded model is the GGUF and aborts otherwise — it passed). `temperature=0.0`, `seed=42`, 3 warm-up iterations discarded per arm, arms run as separate non-interleaved passes.

**Environment:** `Gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF` / `unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF:Q4_K_M` via llama.cpp · SLM checkpoint `specific-AI/email-agent-triage:bert-base-only.gguf` resolved to commit `26dfb379325dd109ee9cc785a32a5565fb017385` · Lemonade 11.0.0 · AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 (Strix Halo), NPU present and deliberately unused · dataset `vendor_corpus_seed.jsonl` sha256 `ff6a54669806334f86212b5fbd7d64cb924e2a5b4b2f4f1b67cac29d3e602bc6`.

**Data quality:** 0 unparsed on either arm, 307/307 scored, per-item rows retained so every aggregate is re-derivable.

**Category assigned to the 57 spam-flagged messages** (this is a category question, not spam detection — neither model was asked "is this spam?"):

| | SLM | Gemma-4-E4B |
|---|---|---|
| PROMOTIONAL | 53 | 54 |
| URGENT | 2 | 3 |
| FYI | 1 | 0 |
| NEEDS_RESPONSE | 1 | 0 |

Both put spam in the right bucket at nearly the same rate. The difference is that the LLM additionally emits an `is_spam` boolean (true on 50/57); the SLM has no such field.

**Ground-truth caveat:** the corpus labels are vendor-supplied and machine-assigned, so these are not absolute accuracy claims about real-world mail. Both arms are scored against the same labels with the same harness, which is what makes the comparison — and a future re-run — valid.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How the three detectors work today, and what the SLM changes (the mechanism write-up this measurement was built on)</summary>

Before running the A/B we traced the three decisions this issue measures. They are not three
instances of one pattern; they are three different architectures, and the SLM lands on each one
differently. **That reorders the test plan, because the cost claim in the Outcome section cannot be
satisfied as the code is currently wired — and the reason is spam.**

### Today, with `GAIA_EMAIL_USE_SLM` off

| Decision | Who decides | Chat LLM on the path? | When the LLM is called |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Category** | Label/keyword rules first, chat LLM otherwise | **Yes** | Per message, when the heuristic is unconfident — on mail carrying no provider category label that is ~97% of it |
| **Phishing** | `detect_phishing` — a fixed keyword/domain pattern list | **No. Never.** | Resolved before any LLM call and never revisited |
| **Spam** | Narrow sender heuristic, chat LLM otherwise | **Yes** | Whenever the heuristic abstains — which it does for essentially every `PROMOTIONAL` message |

Two things here are load-bearing and neither is stated in the issue as written:

**Category and spam are independent escalation triggers.** A message escalates to the chat LLM if
*either* is unresolved. Resolving one does not stop the call.

**Phishing has no LLM call to remove.** It is a pure boolean OR over ~56 hand-maintained patterns,
computed in phase 1 from metadata alone.

### With the flag on

| Decision | Does the SLM change it? | What actually happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Category** | Yes | A BERT classifier runs *between* the heuristic and the LLM; a hit resolves the category |
| **Phishing** | Yes — it **replaces** `detect_phishing` outright | The SLM owns the verdict; the keyword list only backstops a `None` |
| **Spam** | **No — not at all** | Neither checkpoint has a spam label. Still heuristic + chat LLM |

### Why the cost claim cannot land as wired

The issue's own criterion is that a drop in `llm_classified_count` is the SLM's whole cost claim. It
cannot drop, because an SLM category hit satisfies only one of the two escalation conditions. A
`PROMOTIONAL` message whose category the SLM just resolved **still goes to the chat LLM** — for the
spam verdict alone. The call is not removed; only its reason changes.

On phishing the direction is worse. There was never an LLM call on that path, so switching it on
**adds** a model call rather than removing one.

So: **the only axis where the SLM can remove an LLM call is category, and spam blocks it there.**

### Where it should genuinely help

- **Content-driven `URGENT` on the pre-scan surface** — the heuristic never emits `CATEGORY_URGENT`
  and `pre_scan_inbox` passes no chat-LLM classifier, so that category is *structurally* unreachable
  there without the SLM (this is #2771 seen from the other side). This is the SLM's one uncontested
  win, and it is a **capability** gain, not an accuracy gain — worth its own row in the report.
- **Less work in the escalated LLM call** when the category arrives pre-resolved. Real, and worth
  measuring, but a latency/token story rather than a call-count story.

### Where it could be detrimental

- **Phishing precision.** It replaces a heuristic deliberately tuned *for* precision — including a
  29-domain allowlist whose entire job is protecting legitimate senders. The failure mode to watch is
  misflagging genuine account-verification mail (2FA prompts, password resets), exactly the mail
  users least tolerate losing. The committed gate pins five such traps by name.
- **No confidence floor.** Any label the classifier returns is accepted regardless of its score.
- **The classifiers see a ~200-character snippet, not the message body**, and the checkpoint's own
  context is 512 tokens. The vendor's published accuracy was not measured under that constraint.
- **One early failure disables the SLM for the whole process** — the failed build is cached as
  `None`, logged at ERROR, invisible to the caller. An "SLM-on" arm can silently be a second off arm.

## What we found trying to measure it

**The benchmark harness cannot reliably score, and the cause is a self-contradiction in GAIA's own
instructions.** `benchmark.py` prompts the agent *"Call `triage_inbox` …"*, while `triage_inbox`'s
own docstring opens *"Raw per-message classifier. **NOT the tool for 'triage my inbox'** … call
`pre_scan_inbox` instead."* The model obeys the docstring and reroutes — and `pre_scan_inbox` passes
**no classifier at all**, so nothing is scored and no LLM ever runs.

Measured: four full-corpus attempts, all `total_emails: 0`, three of four rerouting to
`pre_scan_inbox`. A 25-message run on the same code *did* route correctly and scored 0.80 — so it is
nondeterministic, not a hard failure.

**None of this is new — it is #2673**, which documented the same contradiction at the same two call
sites on 2026-07-30 and explicitly warns against "fixing" it by editing either side into agreement.

Two things we can add to it:

- **#2673 is almost certainly #2776's unfound suppression point, and neither issue references the
  other.** #2776 reports the classifier "provably never fires" and says the suppression point was
  never located. Rerouting to a classifier-less path produces exactly its reported symptom — 307
  messages in 24 ms with null usage. Linking them closes a question one of them gave up on.
- **On current `main` the misrouting is a coin flip, not deterministic.** #2673 measured it 2/2 at a
  pinned commit. At `abb8ddea` we saw 3 of 4 full-corpus attempts reroute while a 25-message run
  routed correctly — so it may also be scale-sensitive, which matters because it means a small
  smoke-test run can pass while the real run silently fails.

**A measurement-hygiene note for whoever runs this.** `triage_inbox`'s `max_messages` still defaults
to 50 (`read_tools.py:3008-3011` clamps to `min(max_messages or DEFAULT_INBOX_SCAN_MESSAGES,
scan_ceiling)`), so a call without an explicit argument triages 50 while the invocation reads as full
coverage. Pagination itself was fixed in #2634. **Check every scorecard for `total_emails == 307`,
not just `status: PASS`** — which leaves a fair question about whether the committed `--limit 250`
baseline covered 250 messages or 50.

## The blockers, re-checked against the tree

| Blocker | Status | What we found |
|---|---|---|
| **#2771** | **Confirmed** | The pre-scan passes no classifier, and the heuristic never assigns `URGENT` anywhere in its body. Structural. |
| **#2888** | **Confirmed (mechanism)** | The exclusion, the unconditional dependency, and the silent `except → None` are all present. Caveat: the library's own top-level import was inferred from this side, not read directly. |
| **#2776** | **Partially — but not the hard blocker this issue calls it** | The stale ctx envelope is real, now with executed evidence. The id join is intact. "The classifier never fires" is intermittent, and we found its cause (above). |

On #2776, measured rather than argued — a 25-message SLM-off run against a freshly regenerated
corpus scored `category_accuracy` 0.80 and `within_one_bucket` 0.92, joined 25/25 ids (307/308 on a
static whole-corpus check, the one gap being the `_meta` key the loader excludes), and fired the LLM
on 23 of 25 messages with ~44.8k triage tokens. The ctx claim does hold: the first outer-turn call
needed **21,587 input tokens against a 16,384 target**. So Layer 1 does not need #2776 fixed first —
it needs `--ctx-size 32768`, a freshly regenerated corpus, and a call path that doesn't let the model
pick the wrong tool.

## What this changes about the test plan

1. **Spam becomes a measured axis in Layer 1, not a footnote.** It is the mechanism that decides the
   cost result, so a run that doesn't report it cannot explain its own headline number.
2. **Report `llm_classified_count` split by reason** — category-only, spam-only, both. The aggregate
   alone will look flat and hide the whole story.
3. **Give phishing its own cost line.** On that axis the SLM is a net-add.
4. **A live mailbox cannot measure spam at all.** Every scan is scoped to the inbox and the provider
   removed spam upstream, so live spam recall is structurally near-zero — while the corpus's 57 spam
   messages only reach triage because the test backend forces them into the inbox. Live and corpus
   arms measure different populations here and should be reported as such, not compared.
5. **The controls need n≥3 per arm.** Classifier calls are pinned deterministic, but the agent loop
   that picks tools and writes free-form answers sends no temperature at all. A single-run control
   difference cannot be interpreted — and the tool-misrouting above is the same nondeterminism.
6. **`pre_scan_inbox` and `check_suspicious_mail` are the same call.** Prompts 1 and 8 measure one
   surface, not two.
7. **The attention view is structurally immune to the flag** — no classifier of any kind, and it
   filters phishing and spam rows out. If prompt 7 routes there it is a control; if it routes to the
   pre-scan it is the sharpest test in the matrix. Record which, per run.
8. **Drive Layer 1 below the agent loop.** Calling the bulk triage path directly removes the model's
   tool-selection discretion while still exercising the real escalation logic. `POST /v1/email/triage`
   is the complementary surface for per-message accuracy — a different implementation that takes the
   message in the body, needs no mailbox or OAuth, and branches directly on `use_slm`.
9. **Verify the SLM actually loaded before trusting an "on" arm.** Check `slm_build_errors()` is
   empty and that both classifiers return a non-`None` prediction; the cached-`None` path otherwise
   produces a silent second off-arm.

<details>
<summary>🔍 Technical details — call sites and evidence</summary>

**The escalation coupling** — `hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/tools/read_tools.py:1497-1501`:

```python
category_resolved = decision["confident"]
needs_llm = (
    not category_resolved or not heuristic.spam_confident or force_llm
)
escalate = classifier is not None and needs_llm
```

The SLM branch at `:1470-1488` sets `decision["confident"] = True`, `source = "slm"`. It never
touches `heuristic.spam_confident`, so `needs_llm` stays true whenever spam is unresolved.

**Why spam is so often unresolved** — `triage_heuristics.py:210-226`. `_spam_fields` returns
`spam_confident=True` unconditionally for every non-`PROMOTIONAL` category, but for `PROMOTIONAL`
only when `_spam_sender_signal` (`:176-207`) matches a narrow pattern. Ordinary marketing mail
therefore resolves its category confidently and still escalates.

**The ~97% figure** is the codebase's own, at `read_tools.py:1602-1603`: *"a real corpus with no
label signal is majority-unconfident (#2584 — 296/305 messages in the vendor seed corpus)"*.

**Category ladder** — `classify_category_heuristic` (`triage_heuristics.py:364`), first match wins:
PROMOTIONS→PROMOTIONAL `:427`, SOCIAL→PROMOTIONAL `:450`, UPDATES→FYI `:475`, PERSONAL→PERSONAL
`:497`, subject promo keyword `:511`, automated-sender `:528`, IMPORTANT/STARRED→NEEDS_RESPONSE but
*not confident* `:553`, List-Unsubscribe→PROMOTIONAL `:578`, else FYI placeholder *not confident*
`:605`. Any label branch is vetoed back to not-confident when `_has_commitment_signal` (`:331`) finds
a deadline/consequence phrase. `CATEGORY_URGENT` is never assigned anywhere in the function.

**The LLM call** — `classify_email_llm` (`llm_triage.py:259-323`), one call per escalated message,
never batched, `chat.send_messages(..., temperature=0.0)` at `:294-296`, full decoded
reply-stripped body. Only the phase-2 body *fetch* is batched (`read_tools.py:1519-1525`). Cost noted
in-tree as 9–31 s per call (`read_tools.py:1270`).

**Phishing is LLM-free** — `detect_phishing` (`triage_heuristics.py:871-903`) is
`_looks_phishing(subject) or _suspicious_sender_domain(sender) or _looks_phishing_body(body)`. No
score, no threshold, no SPF/DKIM check. Rule counts: 7 subject pairs + 2 phrases (`:131-143`), 29-SLD
allowlist (`:658-691`), 5 suspicious TLDs (`:696`), 30 impersonation brands (`:710-741`), 7 SLD
suffixes (`:766-774`), 1 digit-substitution regex (`:778`), 7 body pairs + 3 body phrases
(`:747-762`). `llm_triage.py`'s structured schema is `{category, is_spam, confidence, reasoning}`
(`:134`) — no `is_phishing` key exists for the LLM to return.

**Spam IS an LLM decision** — `llm_triage.py:122-131` instructs *'set "is_spam" true only for
unsolicited, indiscriminate mass-market junk mail'*; parsed at `:252`; applied only when the
heuristic abstained (`read_tools.py:1558-1559`, `api_routes.py:907-921`).

**Neither checkpoint has a spam target.** `email-agent-triage` emits only
`URGENT/NEEDS_RESPONSE/FYI/PROMOTIONAL/PERSONAL` (`config.py:316-319`, `slm_triage.py:76-98`);
`email-agent-phishing-detection` is strictly binary `"True"/"False"` (`config.py:320-323`,
`slm_phishing.py:6-7,30-32`). Zero spam references in `slm_common.py` or `config.py`.

**Phishing SLM replaces rather than augments** — `read_tools.py:1453-1466` and
`api_routes.py:858-866` run it unconditionally first, with the heuristic's own check disabled up
front (`check_phishing=not phishing_slm_applies`, `read_tools.py:1393`). A `None` falls back to
`detect_phishing` on identical input.

**No confidence gate** — `read_tools.py:1477` is a bare dict-truthiness check; `slm["confidence"]` is
recorded at `:1487-1488` for observability and never compared against a bar.

**Snippet, not body** — both classifiers are passed `msg.get("snippet", "")` (`:1454`, `:1474`),
documented as deliberate at `:1448-1452` to avoid a second round-trip (#2643). This *reverses*
#2568's own note that bulk triage "now decodes full message bodies when the phishing classifier is
wired" — #2643 changed it back.

**Failure caching** — `slm_common.py:42,108-111,147` caches by `(model, checkpoint, base_url)`
*including caching `None`*, so one failed build disables the SLM process-wide.

**`source` undercounts LLM use** — set to `"llm"` only when the LLM resolved *category*
(`read_tools.py:1553`). A spam-only escalation leaves `source="heuristic"` despite an LLM call.
`llm_classified_count = len(call_stats)` (`agent.py:1622`) counts every classify call and is the
honest figure. `EmailTriageResult` (`contract.py:557-605`) carries no `source` field at all.

**Live mailboxes never surface spam** — scans are hard-scoped to the inbox (`read_tools.py:291`,
`_PRE_SCAN_LABEL_IDS` at `:1652`; Outlook always `/me/mailFolders/inbox/messages`,
`outlook_backend.py:463,472`). `grep -n "SPAM\|JUNK\|junkemail"` over both backends returns zero hits
— GAIA excludes spam by never asking, not by reading a provider verdict. The corpus's spam messages
reach triage only because the fake backend stamps every message `INBOX`
(`fake_gmail.py:390-392,220-224`).

**Temperature** — tool-level classification is pinned deterministic (`llm_triage.py:295`,
`calendar_tools.py:485`, `read_tools.py:704`, `summarize_tools.py:170`, `thread_fold.py:139` all
`temperature=0.0`). The agent loop is not: `src/gaia/chat/sdk.py:28` defaults
`temperature: Optional[float] = None` and `:325-326`/`:442-443`/`:546-549`/`:620-623` inject it only
when configured, so an unset value sends none and the backend default applies.

**The hermetic fixture** — `conftest.py:50-72`, autouse, monkeypatches `get_classifier` to `None`
inside both `slm_phishing` and `slm_triage` namespaces. A green unit suite proves the wiring and the
fallback plumbing, and nothing about whether a real classifier returns a correct or even valid
verdict. Opt in with `@pytest.mark.real_slm_build`.

**The misrouting** — `src/gaia/eval/benchmark.py:814` vs `read_tools.py:2980`. `pre_scan_inbox_impl`
passes no `classifier=` to `triage_inbox_impl` (`read_tools.py:2094-2103`), which is why a reroute
yields zero scored messages and zero usage.

**The `max_messages` trap** — `triage_inbox(max_messages: int = DEFAULT_INBOX_SCAN_MESSAGES)` defaults
to 50 (`config.py:110`), separate from the `scan_ceiling` that `GAIA_EMAIL_TRIAGE_MAX_MESSAGES` raises
(`config.py:115-119`); `read_tools.py:3010` computes `min(max_messages or 50, scan_ceiling)`.

</details>


</details>

Harness is committed and re-runnable with a single command, with the environment and dataset hashes recorded, so this can be re-run as the "after" measurement once a spam category ships.

The open question in this issue is answered, and it narrows the problem considerably.

**`sjlab-stx-3` is a Strix Point, not a Strix Halo.** With that, the measured behaviour lines up on SoC rather than on anything box-specific:

| SoC | Runner | EmbeddingGemma 300M loads? |
|---|---|---|
| **Strix Point** | `sjlab-stx-3` | **yes** — `test_embeddings.yml` + `test_rag.yml` green, same model, same helper |
| **Strix Halo** | `sjlab-stx-halo-18` | **no** — fails in every configuration tried |

So this is not a broken machine and not per-box state, as this issue previously speculated. It is a **Strix Halo-specific gap in the llama.cpp embeddings path**: the same model that serves fine on Strix Point cannot start llama-server on Halo, while the *chat* model loads and completes on Halo over that same binary.

**This also rules out the workaround.** Moving the eval to a Strix Point box would fix the embedder and break everything else — Strix Point does not have the 128 GB of unified memory this eval's model assumes, and scores from the two SoCs are not comparable to each other or to the committed baselines. Option 1 in the original description is withdrawn. The only real fix is a Strix Halo backend that can serve embeddings.

#3017 pins the eval to the `strix-halo` label so the wrong-SoC substitution cannot happen by accident, and makes the preflight print `/v1/system-info` so the device and `recipes.llamacpp` backend state are recorded on every run — which is where the Halo-vs-Point backend difference should become visible.

<details>
<summary>🔍 Revised acceptance criteria</summary>

- [x] What differs between the runners — **the SoC**: Strix Point serves this embedder, Strix Halo does not
- [ ] `/v1/system-info` captured on both, with the `llamacpp` backend state and compatible devices diffed — #3017 adds the capture on the Halo side; a Point-side capture still needs collecting from a `test_embeddings.yml` run
- [ ] llama-server's own stderr for the failing load on Halo (needs Lemonade run in a console on the box — CI cannot reach it, see the note in the description)
- [ ] The embedder loads on Strix Halo
- [ ] One completed run with a real scorecard for all three categories against the committed baselines

**Still true and still the blocker:** while this is unfixed, every triggering PR runs the full diagnostic ladder on the Halo box — a 318 MB purge and re-download, 2-3 Lemonade restarts and a global unload, roughly 16 minutes. That box also carries the plain `stx` label, so other `stx` jobs landing there afterwards can hit a cold-model reload; that is the mechanism behind the `test_llm_command_with_server` 60 s timeout seen on 2026-08-19. If this will not be picked up soon, the expensive rungs should be gated behind `workflow_dispatch`.

**Adjacent exposure worth its own decision:** `test_email_agent_eval.yml` and `email_scorecard_refresh.yml` both use `["self-hosted","Windows","stx"]`, so they run on whichever SoC is free — and the second one *refreshes committed baselines*. Left unchanged in #3017 because pinning them trades shared CI capacity.
</details>

comments.body: .take

#3042 is approved and lands most of this, but not the part this issue is named after — so I've changed its link from `Fixes` to `Refs` and I'm leaving this open.

**What #3042 fixes.** `is:unread`, `is:read`, `newer_than:` and `older_than:` now route to Graph's `$filter` instead of being swallowed into a phrase match, and a query mixing a filter operator with a text one fails loudly instead of silently searching half of it. That's acceptance criteria 2, 3 and 4.

**What it doesn't.** Criterion 1 — a `from:` query returning the sender's mail from a connected Outlook mailbox. `from:` and `subject:` come out of #3042 producing the exact same `$search` value `main` already sent, so whatever made operator search come back empty in the original report is still unexplained. The PR went through a round of removing the wrapping quotes and then restoring them, and the restored form is the documented-correct one.

Worth knowing before anyone retests: **Graph never errors on malformed `$search`** — an unrecognised keyword is silently treated as free text. So no mocked test can distinguish a working query from one that quietly degraded to full-text search, and this can only be settled against a real connected mailbox. Nobody on the thread has had one.

**Left to do:**

1. **Verify `from:`/`subject:` against a live Outlook mailbox.** If it works, criterion 1 was never broken and this issue's premise needs correcting. If it doesn't, the cause is somewhere other than quoting and worth chasing on its own.
2. **`label:` is still silently broken.** `label:promotions` goes out as a literal phrase and matches nothing, and it's one of the operators the agent is explicitly told to use.
3. **The agent's own instructions now recommend a query that always errors on Outlook.** The tool description tells the model to combine `from:`, `is:unread` and `newer_than:` in one search; on Outlook that combination is now a hard error by design. The prompt needs to say to split them.

<details>
<summary>🔍 Technical details</summary>

**Criterion 1 — evidence that the request shape is unchanged.** `translate_query` returns `GraphQuery(search=_graph_search_param(query))` for anything with no `is:`/duration operator, and `_graph_search_param` is character-for-character the function `main` already applied:

```
'from:netflix'      main='"from:netflix"'        pr3042='"from:netflix"'        identical=True
'subject:invoice'   main='"subject:invoice"'     pr3042='"subject:invoice"'     identical=True
'from:"Acme Corp"'  main='"from:\"Acme Corp\""'  pr3042='"from:\"Acme Corp\""'  identical=True
```

The Graph `$search` degradation behaviour and the "KQL parses `from:` inside the wrapping quotes" reading come from @kovtcharov-amd's review on #3042, citing [Use the `$search` query parameter](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/search-query-parameter) — Microsoft's own examples are quoted (`$search="from:randiw"`).

**Item 2 — `label:`.** `_IS_RE` and `_DURATION_RE` in `hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/outlook_query.py` are the only operators extracted; everything else falls through to the quoted `$search` string. `label:promotions` is named at `hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/agent.py:505`. Outlook's analogue is `category:`, consistent with `list_labels` mapping master categories — rewriting `label:x` → `category:x` in the search string would close it.

**Item 3 — the prompt.** `hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/tools/read_tools.py:2841` says verbatim: ``Combine them: "from:boss@example.com is:unread newer_than:7d"``. Post-#3042 that query raises `ConnectorsError` on every Outlook search:

```
'from:boss@example.com is:unread newer_than:7d' -> RAISES: search_messages: on Outlook,
    isRead eq false and receivedDateTime ge ... cannot be combined with 'from:boss@example.com'
```

Raising is the right call under the no-silent-fallback rule; the instructions just weren't updated to match.

**Also noted on #3042, not blocking:** `outlook_query.py:72` dereferences `re.fullmatch(...)` without a `None` check. Safe today only because `parse_gmail_duration_value` guarantees the shape — an invariant enforced in a different module.

**Criterion 5** is partially met: `test_outlook_query.py` and `test_outlook_backend.py` pin the request GAIA builds, which is a real improvement over fakes that ignored the query entirely, but per the degradation note above they cannot model Graph's actual parsing.
</details>

Thanks for the detailed follow-up and for narrowing this down. We do not have a live Outlook mailbox to test criterion 1 either, so no help there from us. The label to category mapping and the tool description update both look like small, well-scoped fixes if nobody gets to them first.

Following up on the open `from:` question above — there's a concrete lead, and it's worse than a `from:` problem.

Exchange KQL (the syntax Graph's mail `$search` uses) treats **a space after the colon as a cancellation of the operator**: `to: pilarp` doesn't search the To field, it searches "pilarp" as a plain keyword. Nothing in our pipeline normalizes that, and the operators the model writes are model-generated, so a stray space is a matter of when, not if.

For `from:` that means a silent free-text search. For `is:` and `newer_than:` it's worse — they miss the `$filter` routing entirely and go out as literal phrase text, which is precisely the failure this issue was opened about:

```
'from:netflix'    -> $search='"from:netflix"'
'from: netflix'   -> $search='"from: netflix"'     free-text, not a sender scope
'is: unread'      -> $search='"is: unread"'        never reaches $filter
'newer_than: 7d'  -> $search='"newer_than: 7d"'    never reaches $filter
```

So one space defeats the fix. This is worth checking against the original report — it would explain an empty `from:` result without needing the quoting theory that already turned out to be wrong, and unlike that theory the bottom two lines reproduce without a live mailbox.

The fix is small: make the operator patterns tolerate whitespace after the colon, and pin it with tests.

<details>
<summary>🔍 Technical details</summary>

`_IS_RE` and `_DURATION_RE` in `hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/outlook_query.py` both anchor directly on the colon:

```python
_IS_RE = re.compile(r"\bis:(unread|read)\b", re.IGNORECASE)
_DURATION_RE = re.compile(r"\b(?P<op>newer_than|older_than):(?P<val>\S+)", re.IGNORECASE)
```

`:\s*` in place of `:` in both covers it. `_DURATION_RE`'s `(?P<val>\S+)` already stops at whitespace, so widening the separator doesn't make it swallow the next token. Worth a matching pass on the Gmail side of the query builder if the same assumption is baked in there.

Note this interacts with the mixed-family error: today `is: unread from:alice` does *not* raise, because `is: unread` never registers as a filter operator — it quietly becomes part of the search string. Fixing the regex makes that query start raising, which is the correct behaviour but a visible change.

Docs for the space rule: [Message properties and search operators](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/exchange/policy-and-compliance/ediscovery/message-properties-and-search-operators) — "if there is a space between the name of the property and the search value... the value is just full-text searched". Same page confirms `from:` accepts a display name, SMTP address, or bare domain, so `from:netflix` matching `info@netflix.com` should work once the operator actually survives to Graph.
</details>

Confirmed in code, and thank you for the boundary test — measuring the 40,900 / 41,000 flip is what makes this report actionable rather than anecdotal.

You're right on both halves. GAIA picks its context size from a flat per-device constant (65,536 on the GPU/CPU profile) with no knowledge of the model being loaded, and the "reloaded successfully" message reports the value that was *requested* and echoed back by Lemonade's config — not anything measured against the running llama.cpp slots. So when the two disagree, as they do for a model whose trained context is 40,960, we print the wrong number confidently.

The underlying gap is bigger than the message: GAIA currently has **no source anywhere** for a model's real context ceiling. There's a per-model *minimum* in the registry, but nothing representing a maximum, and nothing reads `n_ctx_train` or queries the live slots. So the clamp you're asking for has nothing to clamp against yet — that's the substance of the fix, not the message wording.

Scope, to set expectations: the default model supports a much larger context, so this bites when a smaller model is selected explicitly, as you did. That makes it a real path, not a hypothetical one — `Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF` ships in GAIA's own model registry.

We're reproducing on a Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S box now to capture what Lemonade's API actually exposes about a model's ceiling, since that determines whether the fix reads it from Lemonade or GAIA has to carry its own table. Will follow up with that result.

<details>
<summary>🔍 Technical details</summary>

- `GPU_CTX_SIZE = 65536` / `NPU_CTX_SIZE = 32768` and `profile_ctx_size()` — `src/gaia/llm/lemonade_client.py:173-184`. Selection is device-only (`src/gaia/cli.py:177`); the model id never enters the decision.
- `_try_reload_with_ctx` (`src/gaia/llm/lemonade_manager.py:869-959`) reloads the resident model to that flat value.
- Both strings you saw come from `src/gaia/llm/lemonade_manager.py:943` and `:946`, gated on `reported_ctx >= min_context_size`, where `reported_ctx` is `all_models_loaded[0].recipe_options.ctx_size` from `/health` — a config echo, not a measurement.
- No occurrences of `n_ctx_train`, `context_length`, `max_position_embeddings`, or a `/slots` query anywhere in `src/gaia/`.
- There *is* a model-aware path — `_ensure_model_loaded_locked` (`src/gaia/llm/lemonade_client.py:3236`) reads `MODELS[...].min_ctx_size`, which is 4096 for this model — but it only corrects upward (`if loaded_ctx >= expected_ctx: return`), so once the startup path has forced 65,536 it never walks it back down. Two individually-reasonable paths composing into the reported behaviour.

Acceptance criteria we're targeting, matching yours: clamp the request to the effective ceiling where one is discoverable, and report the value actually in force rather than the value requested — with a loud warning when the two would differ.
</details>

Following up as promised — reproduced on real hardware, and your numbers hold up precisely.

Test box: Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S, Ubuntu 24.04, GAIA 0.23.0. Measured:

| Measured boundary | GAIA reported | Lemonade echoed | llama.cpp actual |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40,960 | 65,536 | 65,536 | 40,960 (capped) |

Your boundary was right: 40,959 prompt tokens returns 200, 40,960 returns 400 `context_length_exceeded`. And llama.cpp logs exactly the overflow warning you quoted, followed by `the slot context (65536) exceeds the training context of the model (40960) - capping` and `new slot, n_ctx = 40960`.

Two things came out of this that improve the fix:

**The correct number was available all along.** Lemonade's `/api/v1/health` returns `recipe_options.ctx_size: 65536` and `max_context_window: 40960` in the *same payload for the same model*. GAIA reads the first and ignores the second. So the clamp you asked for needs no new data source — just reading a field already in the response.

**The mis-report depends on how the model is loaded.** With an explicit `--model`, a second model-aware path reloads down shortly after, so the wrong number doesn't persist. Without it — which is the common path — nothing corrects it. That explains why this is easy to miss and it's now part of the regression tests.

One note on severity, in case it matters for how you weight it: llama.cpp caps itself and logs it, so there's no unsafe execution at 65,536 — this is purely the reporting-accuracy problem your "What did you expect" section describes, not a stability risk.

Fix is in progress; the PR will link here.

Fix is up in #3003, and your acceptance criteria are met: GAIA now clamps the request to the model's real ceiling and reports the value actually in force.

```
before:  ✅ Context size updated to 65536 tokens.
after:   ⚠️  This model's trained context is 40960 tokens (requested 65536); that is
             the maximum available regardless of configuration.
             Use a model with a larger trained context if you need more.
```

Two things your report led to that weren't in the original diagnosis.

**The correct number was already being delivered to us.** Lemonade returns `max_context_window: 40960` in the same payload as the `ctx_size: 65536` echo, for the same model. GAIA was reading the echo and ignoring the ceiling — so this needed no new data source and no upstream change, just reading the field already in the response.

**The mis-report survived even without a reload.** Clamping only when a reload happens still left it broken for anyone whose model was already resident from an earlier process — the common case, since Lemonade runs as a persistent daemon. The fix now cross-checks every context-size reading, not just post-reload ones.

Thanks for the boundary test in particular. Measuring the 40,900 / 41,000 flip is what made this a diagnosis rather than a report, and the same boundary reproduced exactly on our hardware.

<details>
<summary>🔍 Technical details</summary>

Verified on a Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S box running the reported configuration, plus against a live Lemonade 11.6.0. Measured boundary 40,959 tokens → 200, 40,960 → 400, and llama.cpp's log carried the `n_ctx_seq (65536) > n_ctx_train (40960)` warning, the `- capping` line, and `new slot, n_ctx = 40960` — matching your evidence.

Post-fix numbers: GAIA reports 40960, `max_context_window` 40960, llama.cpp `n_ctx` 40960. The server's `recipe_options.ctx_size` echo is deliberately left untouched at 65536 — GAIA corrects what it reports rather than forcing a reload to make the echo agree, so there's no repeated model reload on the common path.

Scope is as you'd expect from your report: the default model's trained context is well above the profile value, so this only surfaces when a smaller model is selected — which is a real path, and `Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF` ships in GAIA's own registry.

One adjacent issue found and documented but deliberately not fixed here: when switching between models, the pre-flight check inspects the currently-resident model before the switch logic picks the target, so a warning can name the previous model. That ordering predates this change — on `main` it either silently trusts a stale echo or reloads the outgoing model and falsely reports success.
</details>

Diagnosed. This is not a parser bug and not a bad fixture — it is two deliberate decisions meeting, and the fix belongs to **#2805** rather than here.

The C++ corpus gate discovers any `tests/fixtures/*_skills/` directory on purpose, so a new corpus can never be silently ignored. The v0.23.0 merge brought in `tests/fixtures/openclaw_skills/` (PR #2693), and that corpus is deliberately full of *invalid* input — its own `PROVENANCE.md` says the files are verbatim third-party copies, must not be edited, and that "that irregularity is the point of the fixture". So the gate swept in 26 fixtures, and the 13 that are irregular now fail an assertion that says *everything parses cleanly*.

That assertion is the wrong question for this corpus. #2805's actual specification is the right one: run the same corpus through **both** the Python and C++ parsers and assert they reach **identical accept/refuse verdicts** — a design that already expects some fixtures to be correctly refused. That harness does not exist on either side yet.

**Editing the fixtures or "fixing" the parser would both be wrong.** The two real options are to build #2805's verdict-agreement gate, or to land an explicitly-commented interim that narrows the round-trip assertion to the corpus it was written for, with a pointer to #2805 that removes it. That choice belongs to whoever owns the C++ framework-parity plan.

Linking this to #2805 — they were not cross-referenced, which is why the connection was not obvious from either side.

<details>
<summary>Evidence</summary>

**The 52 failures are 13 fixtures × 2 test bodies × 2 platforms.** `SkillCorpus.ParsesAndRoundTrips` and `MetadataOnlyParseKeepsEverythingButTheBody` each run over the discovered corpus. Two distinct, deterministic causes:

- **10 fixtures** — frontmatter `name:` does not match the vendored directory name (e.g. `1password-craftbot/SKILL.md` declares `name: 1password`), rejected by the directory-name gate in `cpp/src/skill.cpp`.
- **3 fixtures** — no YAML frontmatter at all: `doubao-watermark-remover`, `openclaw-security-news`, `openclaw-voice`.

Reproduced locally on macOS/arm64 (`tests_mock --gtest_filter="Fixtures/SkillCorpus.*"` → 26 failures, the same 13 fixture names), matching CI's 26 per platform in run `31679313375`. Not platform-specific.

**The discovery is intentional.** `cpp/tests/test_skill.cpp`'s `isSkillCorpusDir` matches any `*_skills` suffix, and the comment directly above it reads: *"tests/fixtures/openclaw_skills/ adds 26 more when PR #2693 lands. A hardcoded list would silently ignore the new ones."*

The only E4B measurement so far is from the hermetic harness (**5/5**), and this issue exists partly because that harness produced a **false positive** on NPU — 4/5 in the harness against 0/5 live, same commit, same model. A live E4B sweep is running now to answer it.

**Unchanged by the descope:**

- The **harness-vs-sidecar gap** (see the warning in the description) is a real defect regardless of which profile is gated. - The **tool-surface hypothesis** — that a scoped tool is unpickable among ~66 competitors, making this blocked on #2836 rather than solvable by wording — remains the leading explanation and is still untested. **This issue was filed on a live result of "`check_suspicious_mail` selected 0 of 5". That result is an artefact of a blind instrument, and I'm withdrawing it.**

The sweep scored from the sidecar's `tool_call name=…` log lines, which cannot tell the two tools apart:

- `check_suspicious_mail` does not wrap itself in `log_tool_call`; it calls `agent._pre_scan_all_backends(...)` → `pre_scan_inbox_impl`.
- `pre_scan_inbox_impl` wraps its body in `log_tool_call("pre_scan_inbox", …)` — a literal name.

A successful `check_suspicious_mail` call therefore logs as `pre_scan_inbox`. **A run in which the model chose correctly every time would have scored 0/5.** No other answer was reachable.

- **The premise — "the fix does not work on live hardware" — is unproven.** Not disproven; unmeasured.
- **The harness/live divergence described here is not real.** The harness scores from `process_query`'s conversation trace, which records the tool actually chosen, and is the better instrument. Its results (NPU 4/5, E4B 5/5) are the best evidence available and point the other way.
- **The "harness cannot certify this" warning in the description is withdrawn** as stated. The in-process-vs-sidecar gap it invokes is a real concern in general — it has bitten this package repeatedly — but it is not what happened here, and it should not be cited as though it were demonstrated.
- **The tool-surface hypothesis (blocked on #2836) loses its supporting evidence.** It was reasoning from "wording moved the harness but not live"; that contrast has evaporated. It may still be true — but it is now speculation with nothing behind it.

Not "the fix does not work", but **"the fix has never been measured live, because the scoped tool is invisible in the sidecar trace."** The blocking work is:

1. Give `check_suspicious_mail` its own `log_tool_call("check_suspicious_mail", …)` so an invocation is distinguishable. A tool absent from its own trace is hard to debug well beyond this measurement.
2. Re-run the live sweep with a valid instrument.
3. Separately: **no live TUI session on an NPU box can currently be pinned to a non-default model.** `POST /v1/email/agent/session` has no `model_id` field, so `EmailAgentConfig.model_id` stays `None` and `resolve_default_email_model()` always wins — it never consults `gaia config set default_model`. Until step 1 lands, any live number from this sweep is uninterpretable — including a good one.

This issue was filed on "the scoped tool is never selected live — 0/5", which was **retracted** as an instrument artefact. A re-measurement with a working instrument now settles it:

## Update: the ~21s input block is fixed. The root cause underneath it is now isolated, and it is not what this issue's title says.

**The symptom this issue was filed on is resolved.** #2912's `forceLocalAbort` lets a second Esc/Ctrl+C abort locally instead of waiting on the server. Measured live: text typed after that second press reaches the input box in **~70ms**, versus the 18.3–25.2s of dropped keystrokes that prompted this issue.

**But the underlying cause is now measured, and it is bigger than an input-blocking window:**

> **Cancellation cannot interrupt an in-flight LLM generation.**

Confirmed directly on hardware: after cancelling a long free-text prompt, the inference backend kept consuming **~19–20% CPU for over a minute**, and the turn ended minutes later for reasons unrelated to the cancel. The `/cancel` endpoint's own docstring already says as much — *"cooperative, not a kill… the agent loop checks it… stops tool execution."* It stops **tool execution**; it cannot stop a blocking generation call already in flight.

The consequence is a clean split by turn shape:

| turn being cancelled | behaviour |
|---|---|
| has a tool-call step | `Agent run cancelled at step 1/50 via cancel_event`, session frees in ~1s, resend is clean |
| pure free-text generation | nothing to interrupt, lock stays held, resend gets a **409** |

Measured **4 of 8** cancel-then-resends hitting a 409 on a mixed set. An earlier run scored 0/8 using prompts that all reached a tool call early — so that number reflected query selection, not a fix.

### What this issue should become

Not "input blocks ~21s" — that is fixed. The real item is: **a cancelled free-text turn holds its session lock until generation completes on its own, so a prompt resend legitimately conflicts.**

Plausible directions, none obviously right:
- Interrupt generation at the backend (may not be supported by the local inference runtimes)
- Accept that the lock is held and make the client absorb it — queue the resend and dispatch when the session frees, so the user never sees a 409 even though one would have occurred
- Accept the 409 as correct, since it *is* an accurate statement of server state, and treat the actionable message #2912 added as the complete fix

The third is defensible. This constraint is **pre-existing** and not something #2912 introduced — that PR made every occurrence say something useful instead of "check `gaia daemon status`", and removed the frozen-UI window that made it feel like a hang.

| Symptom | Result |
|---|---|
| Stale ctx envelope | **Confirmed.** The first outer-turn call needed **21,587 input tokens against a 16,384 target** — 5,203 over — before any classify call ran |
| Predicted↔ground-truth id join has zero overlap | **Not reproduced.** 25/25 in the run; 307/308 on a static whole-corpus check, the single gap being the `_meta` key that `_labelled_ids()` deliberately excludes. `generate_mbox.py` and `FakeGmailBackend` derive ids through the same `mbox_message_to_gmail_payload` path, so a fresh regen aligns by construction. The real hazard is a **stale** pair — `ensure_corpus()` checks existence only, no hashing, and both files are gitignored |
| Classifier never fires | **Intermittent, cause = #2673.** A 25-message run routed to `triage_inbox` correctly and scored `category_accuracy` 0.80 with `llm_classified_count` 23/25 and ~44.8k triage tokens. Four full-corpus attempts on the same code returned `total_emails: 0`, three of them having rerouted to `pre_scan_inbox` |

`pre_scan_inbox_impl` passes no `classifier=` to `triage_inbox_impl` (`read_tools.py:2094-2103`), which is why a reroute yields zero scored messages and zero usage.

Note the scale asymmetry: the 25-message run routed correctly while the 307-message runs mostly did not. #2673 measured the reroute as deterministic at its pinned commit; on `abb8ddea` it behaves as a coin flip. Worth knowing, because a small smoke-test run can pass while the real run silently fails.

Practical consequence for #3095, which names this issue a hard prerequisite for its whole Layer 1: with `--ctx-size 32768`, a freshly regenerated corpus, and a call path that removes the model's tool choice, the harness does produce real numbers today.
</details>

### Corpus blocker is being solved

The "J1 and J3 aren't testable yet" problem above is being addressed directly: a 21-thread /
46-message corpus of real human conversations, ground-truthed by construction, is being sent
into the test Gmail account, plus calendar invites for J4. It carries the Gmail label
`GAIA-EVAL/corpus-v2`, so `-label:GAIA-EVAL/corpus-v2` recovers the pre-existing view — which
is the isolation-and-documentation requirement this issue asked for, and the thing the old
`GAIA-FIXTURE` mail never had.

Ground truth built before this lands (including `ground-truth-v0`) goes stale the moment it
does.

### Two structural facts about J1, verified in code

Both surfaced while building that corpus. Both change what J1 can be held to.

**1. The heuristic layer can never confidently produce an actionable category.** Every
`confident=True` return in [`triage_heuristics.py`](hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/tools/triage_heuristics.py)
is `PROMOTIONAL` (×4), `FYI` (×2) or `PERSONAL` (×1) — lines 423, 449, 477, 490, 505, 534, 586.
There is **no** confident path to `URGENT` or `NEEDS_RESPONSE`; the `NEEDS_RESPONSE` return at
`:548` is explicitly `confident=False` with reason `"escalating to LLM"`.

So J1 — "what needs me?", the core job of this agent — is the one place where the design rule
at the top of this issue *cannot currently be satisfied*. The tool can confidently tell you
what to ignore; deciding what needs you is delegated to the model layer, which is precisely
the layer today's evidence says fabricates. J1's bar is unchanged, but meeting it likely
requires moving some URGENT/NEEDS_RESPONSE determination into the tool, not better prompting.

**2. `waiting_on_you` requires in-thread corroboration, so a cold inbound ask is suppressed.**
[`waiting_on_you_tools.py:202-205`](hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/tools/waiting_on_you_tools.py#L202):
either ≥2 prior messages from the user in that thread, or one prior message that passes a
substance check.

**This is deliberate, not a defect** — the module docstring (`:34-104`) records three
successive checkpoint fixes hardening it after an adversarial verifier manufactured
corroboration to get every marketing email from an address flagged as awaiting a reply.
Loosening it trades directly against that attack.

It is still a real recall gap for J1: a genuine first-contact ask from someone you've never
emailed will not appear. That is a product decision to make deliberately, not a bug to file —
and the corpus should ground-truth cold inbound asks explicitly so the tradeoff is measured
rather than assumed.

### J2 scoping fact: the agent is multi-mailbox in enumeration, single-mailbox in reasoning

Follow-on to the corroboration note above, and a distinct failure class from the deliberate
recall cost described there.

[`waiting_on_you_tools.py:548`](hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/tools/waiting_on_you_tools.py#L548)
iterates `for provider, backend in agent._backends.items()` and passes
`detect_waiting_on_you_impl` a **single** backend client (`:262`), whose only corroboration
path is `get_thread` on that same backend (`:274`). Each mailbox is therefore scanned in
complete isolation.

Consequence: a two-sided conversation split across mailboxes — the inbound sitting in Gmail,
the user's substantive reply sent from Outlook — fails the corroboration bar not because
corroboration is absent but because the scan cannot reach it. The trade-off documented at
`:34-104` justifies rejecting *manufactured* corroboration; it says nothing about discarding
real corroboration for bookkeeping reasons.

This is deterministic, not probabilistic — it reproduces on every run. It also compounds the
budget split already noted for `triage_inbox` (`agent.py:1351`) and `search_messages`
(`read_tools.py:2229`), where a second connected mailbox silently halves the window the
agent sees per backend.

Ground truth for J2 must therefore state which mailbox each side of a thread lives in, or
the expected result is unknowable.

### J4's baseline has moved — three real calendar events now exist

Three Google Calendar events landed on the test account on 2026-08-03: a design review
(Thu 06 Aug 09:00), a deliberate conflict (Wed 05 Aug 10:30–11:30) and a board meeting
(Thu 13 Aug 14:00). Calendar only — the conversation corpus itself has **not** been sent, so
every mail-derived count on this issue is still current.

J4 drew its diagnostic power from a ground truth of **zero**: with no invites anywhere, any
answer other than "none" was unambiguously a fabrication, which is how the last run caught the
TUI inventing five meetings with invented attendee names. That baseline no longer holds
unconditionally, and the split now matters:

- `detect_meeting_request` over **mail** — still zero, provided the events did not generate
  invite emails into the inbox. Pending confirmation.
- `list_calendar_events` / `detect_calendar_conflicts` over **calendar** — now nonzero, with
  a purpose-built conflict on 05 Aug.

If mail stayed at zero this is a net improvement: fabrication and recall get tested on
separate branches instead of sharing one. If invite mail did land, the zero-truth view must
stay recoverable via `-label:GAIA-EVAL/corpus-v2`.

Either way, J4's grounding bar ("every date, time and attendee in the answer exists in a real
record") now has real records to check against, so those three events must be in the corpus
ground truth with their times and attendees.

**Resolved — calendar-only. J4's zero mail baseline is intact.**

Verified by search rather than inferred from the create call, since it is an absence claim:
`from:calendar-notification@google.com OR filename:ics` returns nothing over the period, and a
sweep for "invitation OR invite OR Board meeting" returns only pre-existing newsletters
matching incidentally. Structural reason: no attendees were ever set on the three events, so
Google had nobody to notify.

So J4 splits the way we wanted — `list_calendar_events` has a nonzero truth of 3,
`detect_calendar_conflicts` has a real overlap on 05 Aug 10:30–11:30, and mail-side
`detect_meeting_request` keeps its zero. Recall and fabrication on separate branches.

The empty attendee lists give J4 a sharper grounding rule than the one written above:
**no event has any attendee, so any attendee name appearing in an answer is fabricated, with
no interpretation required.** That is a direct probe for the exact defect seen on 2026-08-03,
where five meetings were reported with invented attendee names.

### Corpus has landed — every mail-derived count above is stale

43 messages across 20 threads were delivered to the test Gmail account on 2026-08-03 between
23:32 and 23:57 UTC; inbox unread went 638 → 665, nothing in Spam. Ground truth predating that
window — including `ground-truth-v0` and the "100% newsletters" characterisation this issue
was written against — no longer describes the mailbox.

**Baseline exclusion requires BOTH labels:**

```
-label:GAIA-EVAL/corpus-v2 -label:GAIA-FIXTURE
```

The corpus carries the first. The second is pre-existing synthetic mail, and it is far larger
than previously understood: **406 messages** in Gmail. (The "24 GAIA-FIXTURE messages" recorded
during the last run was a different measurement entirely — 24 of the 25 messages in the
*Outlook* backend's scan window were synthetic. Gmail label cardinality and an Outlook window
count are not comparable, and neither supersedes the other.) Excluding only the corpus label
still leaves 406 synthetic messages in view.

**Consequence for windowing.** 43 messages arriving at the top of the inbox means the corpus
now dominates the agent's 50-message triage window, and `search_messages` (window 25) will be
operating almost entirely on corpus mail. That is what we wanted for J1 and J3, but
pre-corpus newsletter behaviour is no longer observable in the same run — the two baselines
have to be taken separately, via the label filter.

**Known corpus caveats**, all recorded in the corpus's own `DELIVERY.md`:

- Two threads duplicated by a mid-send disconnect (A3 ×3, N1 ×2). Left in place — identical
  copies, graded signals unaffected; only per-thread message counts are wrong.
- One thread split into two Gmail threads by subject grouping (a `Re:` prefix on one side), so
  it legitimately yields two follow-up candidates rather than one.
- Time-based threads are stamped on delivery day, so the follow-up cases only become live on
  or after **2026-08-06**. Grading them before that date measures nothing.
- Four threads are degraded because every persona shares one envelope sender: two needed an
  automated `no-reply@`/`alerts@` sender, two needed a `List-Unsubscribe` header that Graph
  strips. One further thread was withheld entirely, because opt-out suppression keys on sender
  address and sending it would have suppressed `waiting_on_you` corpus-wide.

An unresolved discrepancy in the delivery report — 20 threads vs 33 labelled conversations —
is being reconciled before any run is graded. It matters for J2 specifically: `check_followups`
scans SENT, so whether the Sent side is counted separately changes that job's expected result.

### J2 grading basis — decided: grade against the mailbox, not against corpus intent

The corpus sends carried no `In-Reply-To`/`References`, so Gmail grouped them on subject alone
and did so **inconsistently** — some of the user's replies threaded with the persona message,
others became standalone conversations. A 3-message logical thread can appear as 1, 2 or 3
Gmail conversations, and 20 logical threads became 33 conversations (14 of them SENT).

The consequence lands on J2: **six** conversations have a message from the user as their
latest with no reply — two by design, four as threading artifacts.

**Decision: the expected answer is 6. Reporting 2 is a failing answer.**

The agent sees Gmail conversations, not the send list. It has no observable signal
distinguishing an artifact from a designed case — in both, the user sent last and nobody
replied, which is a true statement about the mailbox. An agent reporting 2 would be inventing
a distinction it cannot perceive, which is the same class of failure J2 exists to catch.

| reported | verdict |
|---|---|
| 6 | correct enumeration — pass |
| 2 | fail — it cannot know that |
| 3, 4, 5 | the #2622 dropout signature |

The four artifacts stay named in the corpus's `DELIVERY.md` — not to exclude them from the
grade, but so a future reader doesn't mistake a correct 6 for corpus corruption.

Worth stating: inconsistent threading is not damage. Real mailboxes are full of replies that
failed to thread because a client dropped `In-Reply-To`. This makes J2 more realistic than the
designed version.

### The arithmetic trap this creates

**J2's expected value must not be computed as "yesterday's 22 + 6".** Two independent reasons:

1. The corpus **adds to** the pre-existing waiting-on set rather than replacing it.
2. `check_followups` windows on **50 SENT messages**, not 50 threads — the 14 new SENT messages
   push 14 older ones out of that window, so an unknown number of yesterday's 22 have silently
   fallen off the bottom.

The expected value has to be **recomputed on the box against the same window the agent will
see**, immediately before each run. Yesterday's 22 was only trustworthy because it was derived
that way; the 6/6 result means nothing otherwise.

### J2 gains a second, sharper check: `scan_truncated`

[`followup_tools.py:176`](hub/agents/email/python/gaia_agent_email/tools/followup_tools.py#L176)
sets `scan_truncated` when the SENT listing returns a `nextPageToken` or fills the 50-message
ceiling, and it is surfaced in the envelope (`:235`, `:241`, `:341`), so it reaches the model.
Because the corpus pushes the Sent side toward that ceiling, the flag should now be observable
in practice rather than theoretical.

Two things follow.

**1. It disambiguates J2's failure mode.** A short count can now be attributed rather than
guessed: `scan_truncated: false` with a short list is the #2622 model-dropout signature;
`scan_truncated: true` means the tool itself never saw the rest. Previously both looked
identical from the answer alone.

**2. It is a direct test of the "no silent degradation" bar.** The flag is in the envelope, so
an agent that presents a truncated scan as a complete answer is failing that bar with the
evidence sitting in its own input.

The code comment at `:172-175` makes this materially worse than generic truncation, and it
should be quoted in any finding:

> the listing is newest-first, so hitting the cap means the OLDEST (most overdue) sends are the
> ones left unscanned

So a truncated J2 answer is not merely incomplete — it is **biased against precisely the items
the user most needs**, dropping the longest-overdue follow-ups while confidently presenting the
recent ones. "You have N things awaiting a reply," silently omitting the oldest, is a worse
outcome than an error.

**Added to J2's bar:** when `scan_truncated` is true, the agent must say so. Presenting a
truncated scan as exhaustive fails the job regardless of how many rows it got right.

## Corpus is seeded — all four jobs are now exercisable, but read the five traps first

The mailbox is no longer 100% newsletters. Measured against live Gmail just now:
**47 messages / 33 Gmail threads / 21 logical conversations**, 14 of them sent by the account
owner. It has real asks with hard deadlines, two phishing lures written in urgent-action
language, a personal thread, explicitly-no-action-needed mail, and marketing. J1 and J3 were
blocked on exactly this and are now unblocked.

**Five corpus properties will silently corrupt a ground truth if you don't apply them.** Each
was verified against the mailbox, not inferred. Two of them change what a *correct* answer is,
so they must be settled before any expected value is computed — not after a run disagrees.

### The five traps

| | What's wrong | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **1. The label name is doubled** | Display name is `GAIA-EVAL/corpus-v2GAIA-EVAL/corpus-v2`, not `GAIA-EVAL/corpus-v2` | `label:GAIA-EVAL/corpus-v2` returns **zero threads**. The baseline-exclusion query recorded on this issue matches nothing and fails open — every "baseline" measurement silently includes the corpus. Use the id `Label_6155903793123680676`. |
| **2. Two conversations are chronologically scrambled** | In thread `19fc9fe8d9203d59` the `Re:` reply is stamped **23:38:45**, 2m15s *before* the message it answers at **23:41:00**. Same in the personal thread — the answer precedes the question. | J3 has no coherent narrative for *Q4 budget* or *dinner on the 14th*. Ordering by timestamp yields nonsense, so a wrong-looking summary there is the corpus's fault, not the agent's. The other 8 conversations are clean. |
| **3. Gmail split 10 conversations into 22 threads** | Same-subject messages landed in separate `threadId`s — *Q4 budget* alone spans **4** threads | `get_thread` can only ever return a fragment. And it inflates J2: two sent messages that **were** answered look unanswered because the answer sits in a different thread. |
| **4. Three "attachments" don't exist** | "Packet attached", "revised SOW attached", "Attaching the ingestion rewrite spec" — `has:attachment` across the corpus returns **zero** | Good news, actually: `has:attachment` has a precise correct answer, and any claim about attachment *contents* is a clean fabrication catch. |
| **5. Personas exist only in signature blocks** | Every corpus message is from `tomasz.testingiewicz@outlook.com`; Marcus, Sofia, Dana, Tom, Priya, Roz and Ines appear only in body text | `J3.b`/`J3.c` ("your conversation with *person*") can't resolve a person to an address. Person attribution comes from body prose — the exact surface where fabrication happens. Sharper probe, but the phrasings need to name people as the bodies do. |

Traps 2 and 3 are worth re-seeding for; 1 is a one-line label rename; 4 and 5 are fine as-is
and arguably improve the corpus.

### What each job can now measure

<details>
<summary>J1 — 8 items genuinely need a reply, 12 must not be surfaced</summary>

**Needs a reply:** Fieldstone MSA counter-signature (hard Friday 5pm ET stop, plus an explicit
chase) · SEV1 replica down, no owner assigned · Northgate phase 2 (sender is *blocked* pending
Tomasz's answer on the primary region) · revised deck (3 slides on placeholder data awaiting
his numbers) · partnership intro (client asked him by name to lead) · 30-minutes call (3 slots
offered) · cold intro from Ines · dinner on the 14th (personal).

**Must not be surfaced:** two phishing lures — *"Your account has been suspended — click here
to verify"* and *"Action required: unusual sign-in"* — both written in the same urgent-action
register as the real asks. This is the precision test the old corpus could not do at all: an
agent that keys on urgency words rather than a genuine ask will promote both. Plus "v3 endpoint
is live — **no action needed**", FYI cutover notes, three conversations Tomasz already closed
out, two marketing sends, and a connectivity-check stub.

One judgment call to settle before grading: the failing nightly CI build is actionable but
addressed to nobody in particular.
</details>

<details>
<summary>J2 — the expected value moved, and trap 3 makes two answers defensible</summary>

14 new sent messages entered the 50-message `SENT` window, displacing 14 older ones. The
previous expected value of 22 is **void** — recompute on-box against the exact window
immediately before each run, and never as "22 + n": the corpus *displaces*, it doesn't add.

Then trap 3 bites: a literal per-thread scan reports at least two sent messages as awaiting a
reply that were in fact answered in a sibling thread. Decide which is being graded — the
literal count or the user-meaningful one — **before** the run.

`scan_truncated` still applies as the second check, per the earlier comment.
</details>

<details>
<summary>J3 — 8 clean conversations, and trap 3 is the structural test</summary>

*Q4 budget* is 6 messages across 4 Gmail threads. Ask "where did we land on the Q4 budget?"
and any single `get_thread` sees at most 2 of them — so the honest answers are either the full
6-message arc or a stated inability to see it all. Confidently summarising from a 2-message
fragment is the failure. Skip this pair for chronology grading (trap 2); the other 8 are sound.
</details>

<details>
<summary>J4 — the zero-ground-truth probe is gone, replaced by two sharper ones</summary>

Time-sensitive mail now exists, so "any answer other than none is a fabrication" no longer
holds and that wording has been corrected in the issue body. Replacing it: **proposals are not
invites** — three emails offer times and one claims "invite sent", but the corpus contains no
calendar invite and no attachment at all, so `J4.c` has a precise correct answer. And **any
attendee name is fabricated** — the three real calendar events all carry empty attendee lists.
</details>

### Also changed since this issue was opened

`main` is now at `e135b8ef`. **#2756 is fixed and merged (#2760)** — and the fix was exactly
the design rule at the top of this issue: the tool precomputes `count`, the model states it

#2621 is closed. #2759 remains open and still feeds J1.

One more unfiled finding, added to the list above: a PR stacked on a feature branch never
triggers the email suites, because `test_email_agent.yml` filters `pull_request:
branches: [main]` on the PR *base* — and the checks page still looks healthy. That's a third
