Adding a **correctness** argument for keeping the card heuristic-derived, distinct from the cost argument this issue was filed on. It should be visible to anyone later weighing "should we add the rich version back?"

Independent validation work on the same agent (#2511 campaign) measured the agent **fabricating** message content, not merely dropping it:

- Thread reconstruction duplicated one message and replaced another with a repeat of an earlier one — 2 of 8 effectively lost.
- A sender was misattributed.
- A timestamp of "11:40 AM" was invented and rendered identically by two independent surfaces, despite appearing nowhere in the source.
- A separate run fabricated five meeting requests with invented human names against a ground truth of **zero**.

**Fabrication is a different severity class from incompleteness.** A dropped row is visibly incomplete and a user discounts it. An invented timestamp or an invented sender name is indistinguishable from truth at the point of use.

This matters more in a card than in chat. Chat prose reads as the model talking and gets discounted accordingly; **a card reads as data and does not.** The same fabricated value is more dangerous rendered in a bordered row under a `NEEDS YOU` header than in a sentence.

The shipped fast-and-thin card is *structurally* incapable of this failure: every displayed field — sender, subject, age, and the category reason from `triage_heuristics.py` — comes from message metadata or a deterministic heuristic. **No displayed field passes through generation.** The version pulled here would have put LLM-extracted prose in every row.

So any future implementation of per-row detail carries a requirement neither shape above states explicitly:

- [ ] Extracted detail must be **attributable to source text**, not merely plausible. A quoted deadline or a proposed time should be verifiable against the message body — if it cannot be located there, it is not shown.
- [ ] Detail is visually distinguishable from heuristic-derived fields, so a reader can tell which parts of a row are extracted and which are metadata.

The on-demand shape (option 1) is also the safer one on this axis: the user has explicitly asked about one specific row, so extracted content arrives as an answer to a question rather than as ambient data in a table they are scanning.

Credit for the measurements to the session running the T-series validation; raised here rather than left in that campaign's index because it changes the design constraints on this issue, not just its priority.

Measured this live on a real draft PR (#2782) while working on a different issue, and the close/reopen remedy described here doesn't work on its own — worth correcting before someone else relies on it.

**Close/reopen alone: does not re-run gated jobs.** `reopened` is a listed workflow trigger, so the workflow itself does fire — but every job's own `if:` still evaluates independently:

```
github.event_name != 'pull_request' || github.event.pull_request.draft == false || contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'ready_for_ci')
```

For a `reopened` action on a draft PR: `event_name` is still `'pull_request'` (false), `draft` is unchanged by reopening (still `true`, so `draft == false` is false), and there's no label yet (false). All three false → every job skips. Checked directly with `gh pr checks` right after the reopen: everything read `skipping`, not `pending`/`pass`.

**The working manual path: add the `ready_for_ci` label FIRST, then close and reopen.** Label alone doesn't work either (this issue's actual bug — `labeled` isn't a trigger type, so nothing re-fires). But label-then-reopen combines correctly: the reopen fires the workflow, and by then the label is present, so `contains(labels, 'ready_for_ci')` is true and the job gate passes. Confirmed on #2782 — after adding the label and closing/reopening, the previously-skipping jobs (Email Agent Unit Tests, Test Email Agent, Run Code Quality Checks, Security Tests, Unit Tests, etc.) all switched to `pending`/running, with the PR still draft.

Until #2767 lands, this repo's actual manual workaround is **label + reopen**, not reopen alone.

title: fix(ci): ready_for_ci label does not re-trigger skipped jobs — 'labeled' is not a PR trigger type

comments.body:
Stress-tested this against the GAIA codebase and against Hermes Agent, the closest real-world implementation of a self-improving agent. **The architecture survives, but one core claim above is wrong and must be corrected before any work starts.**

## Correction: mutability must follow provenance, not be a global rule

The issue states "nothing ever writes to the authored file" as a blanket policy. That is right for *authored* skills and wrong for *synthesized* ones — and GAIA has both.

Hermes takes the opposite approach to what I proposed: it mutates skill files directly. Skills are created autonomously after complex tasks, then patched in place when outdated, incomplete, or wrong, and archived rather than deleted. There is no immutable base or overlay anywhere in its design.

That is not a flaw in Hermes — it is correct *for Hermes*, because its skills are self-generated. There is no third-party original to protect, so a pristine base would be protecting nothing. GAIA's milestone-60 skills are different: authored by a person, installable from the hub, and subject to upstream version updates. There, the base genuinely must not be clobbered.

So the rule becomes:

| Skill origin | Mutability | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Synthesized (`provenance.source == 'synthesized'`) | Mutable | Supersede lineage — **already built** |
| Authored / hub-installed | Immutable base | Learned overlay — the new work |

Applying an overlay to the synthesized corpus would be strictly worse than what ships today.

## The bigger finding: most of the "overlay store" already exists

The `procedures` table (`memory_store.py:283`) is more capable than this issue assumed:

```
provenance      TEXT    -- JSON {source:'synthesized', from_sessions:[...]}
version         TEXT
enabled         INTEGER -- disable without delete (blocks recall)
success_count   INTEGER
attempt_count   INTEGER -- success_count/attempt_count = success rate
superseded_by   TEXT    -- set on supersede; old row KEPT, never deleted
embedding       BLOB    -- over when_to_use, its own FAISS index
last_used_at    TEXT
```

And `reconcile_and_store` (`skill_synthesis.py:653`) already implements ADD / UPDATE / NOOP, matching **by meaning** — `when_to_use` embedding cosine ≥ τ — rather than by name, precisely because the distiller authors a fresh name each pass and a name match would duplicate instead of supersede (#1818). UPDATE inserts a new row and marks the old `superseded_by` it (Zep lineage). **No path ever DELETEs.**

That is insert-new-then-supersede with full lineage — immutable *history* with a mutable *head*. It is the same guarantee the overlay was invented to provide.

**This answers the "one store or two?" open question: one.** Extend `procedures`; do not build a second store. Building a parallel overlay table would have been the expensive mistake, and this issue as originally written pointed straight at it.

## Where Hermes independently validates the design

Hermes gates skill writes behind `skills.write_approval`: when enabled, every create/edit/patch/delete **stages** rather than applies, queued for review via `/skills pending` with unified diffs (`/skills diff <id>`), and on messaging surfaces changes stay out-of-band until explicitly approved. Nous calls it a consent-aware learning loop.

That is the same control this issue requires for untrusted deltas, arrived at independently by a shipped product. Strong signal that the confirmation gate is not over-engineering — it is the minimum viable safety control for self-modifying agents. **Adopt the staging model explicitly**, including reviewable diffs, rather than a bare yes/no prompt.

## Where GAIA is already ahead of Hermes — preserve this

Hermes patches a skill when the model judges it "outdated, incomplete, or wrong." That is a model judgment call, and a confidently wrong model degrades the skill with nothing to stop it.

GAIA supersedes on `success_count` — an **empirical track record**, not an opinion. A candidate only wins if its cluster demonstrably outperformed the incumbent. That is materially more robust against self-degradation, and it is the single best property of the existing design.

**v2 must keep empirical dominance as the promotion rule for learned changes.** Do not replace it with model judgment to match Hermes.

## Two genuine gaps Hermes exposes

1. **No consolidation/umbrella merge.** Hermes extracts the core steps of similar micro-skills and merges them into a master `SKILL.md` umbrella. GAIA's reconcile does ADD/UPDATE/NOOP against a *single* match — it supersedes but never consolidates several related procedures into one. Without this, a long-lived agent accumulates near-duplicate procedures that each individually clear τ against different neighbours. Worth a sub-issue.

2. **Decay is unimplemented.** `last_used_at` exists but is **telemetry only** — stamped on recall so `gaia memory status` can report reuse (`procedural_memory.py:279`), with no consumer for pruning or ranking. This resolves the "do deltas expire?" open question: the data is already there, nothing uses it. Decay is a scoping decision, not a schema change.

Also worth noting Hermes triggers autonomous skill creation after complex tasks (5+ tool calls) — a concrete, cheap heuristic against GAIA's cluster-based synthesis. Not necessarily better, but a useful comparison point when tuning when learning fires.

## Net effect on the decomposition above

- **Item 1 (overlay store + delta grammar)** shrinks substantially — extend `procedures` with an overlay/delta discriminator and an anchor to a base skill, rather than designing a store from scratch.
- **Item 3 (write path)** should adopt Hermes' staged-with-diff review model explicitly.
- **Item 4 (rebase)** is unaffected and remains the hardest genuinely-new problem: nothing in either codebase re-anchors a learned change when an authored base updates, because Hermes has no authored base to update against. **This is the part with no prior art to copy — treat it as the highest-risk item.**
- **Add:** consolidation/umbrella merge, and a decay policy for `last_used_at`.
- **Open question "one store or two" — resolved: one.**

Sources: [Hermes Agent — Persistent Memory](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/memory/) · [Hermes Agent docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/) · [NousResearch/hermes-agent](https://github.com/nousresearch/hermes-agent)

## Design direction: push learning *down the stack*, not into the prompt

Hermes encodes everything it learns as **prose in a skill file**, which is then injected into context. That is the right call for a model-agnostic agent typically driving a frontier model with a large window. It is the wrong call for GAIA's target, and the constraint is what gives GAIA a chance to do better rather than merely different.

### The constraint that creates the opportunity

GAIA's local envelope, from the shipped code:

| Constraint | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| NPU context ceiling | **32,768** tokens | `NPU_CTX_SIZE`, `lemonade_client.py:174` |
| GPU/CPU context | 65,536 | `GPU_CTX_SIZE`, `:173` |
| Default model | **Gemma-4-E4B** (~4B params) | `DEFAULT_MODEL_NAME`, `:124` |
| Tool budget | **14** (11 CORE + 3 dynamic) | `DEFAULT_MAX_TOOLS`, `tool_loader.py` |
| Recall body cap | 1,500 chars | `MAX_RECALL_BODY_CHARS`, `skill_synthesis.py:65` |

Prose-as-learning does not fit this. A dozen learned skills at even 500 tokens each consumes a meaningful fraction of a 32K window that already holds the system prompt, tool schemas, RAG chunks, and conversation. And on an NPU, re-prefilling that window is far more painful than on a datacenter GPU — which is exactly why `ToolLoader` is deliberately monotonic so non-expansion turns serialize byte-identically and the KV prefix cache stays warm.

### The proposal: tiered learning, cheapest representation wins

Most of what an agent actually learns is **not prose**. "This sender matters," "for this goal use these four tools," "escalate above this threshold" are structured facts wearing a sentence as a costume. Encode them structurally and they cost nothing.

| Tier | What it holds | Resident context cost | Example |
|:--:|---|:--:|---|
| **0 — Data** | Facts the *tools* query directly | **zero** | sender-importance scores read by the ranking tool |
| **1 — Selection** | Tool priors per goal | **zero added text** | goal → `tools_required`, already `ToolLoader`'s `SKILL` term |
| **2 — Parameters** | Typed knobs bound to a skill section | tens of tokens | thresholds, orderings, category lists |
| **3 — Prose** | Genuinely procedural knowledge | hundreds | how to word an escalation |

**The governing rule: learning is recorded at the lowest tier that can represent it. Prose is the fallback, never the default.** Hermes only has tier 3.

Tier 0 is the significant one and it is nearly free. If "which senders matter" lives in a table the ranking tool reads, the agent gets measurably better at *your* mail with **zero prompt growth**. Hermes structurally cannot do this — its learning lives in files destined for the context window. GAIA can, because it already has a tool layer between the model and the work.

Tier 1 is already built. `ToolLoader` admits a recalled procedure's `tools_required` as the `SKILL` term at precedence `CORE > SKILL > SEMANTIC`, cap-bound with no bundle pull-in. Learning which tools solve which goal changes *which schemas render*, not how much text is added.

### Three further consequences of being local

**1. Empirical gating is mandatory, not merely preferable.** Hermes patches a skill when the model judges it "outdated, incomplete, or wrong." A 4B local model is a substantially worse self-judge than a frontier model, so importing that design would be actively unsafe here. GAIA's existing `success_count` / `attempt_count` dominance rule is the correct promotion gate *because* the model is small — track record does not depend on the model's introspective accuracy.

**2. Prefix stability is a hard requirement.** Deltas apply at **session boundaries only**, never mid-turn. Mutating learned content inside a session changes the prompt prefix and invalidates the KV cache, and on NPU that re-prefill cost will exceed whatever the learning saved.

**3. A learning budget, enforced.** Tier-2 and tier-3 learning gets a hard token ceiling. At the ceiling, consolidation runs (the umbrella-merge gap identified from Hermes) or the lowest-value entries are demoted to retrieval-only. Unbounded accumulation is a slow context leak, and on 32K it is fatal rather than untidy. `last_used_at` already exists as the ranking signal and currently has no consumer.

### Retrieval over residency

Tier 3 should follow the progressive-disclosure model milestone 60 already ships: learned prose stays **retrievable, not resident**, surfacing only when its trigger embedding matches. The FAISS index over `when_to_use` that `reconcile_and_store` maintains is exactly this mechanism, already built.

### Where this genuinely beats Hermes

- **Learning that costs no context** (tiers 0–1) is unavailable to a file-and-prose design.
- **Promotion gated on measured success** rather than model self-assessment — more robust generally, and necessary with a 4B model.
- **Bounded, typed deltas** are inspectable and revertible individually; a prose patch is not.
- **Privacy as capability:** local execution means learning from full message content carries no exfiltration risk, so GAIA can learn from material a cloud agent must avoid persisting. This raises the injection stakes correspondingly — the staged-diff consent gate adopted from Hermes is what makes it safe to exercise.

### Where Hermes stays ahead

Prose is more expressive, and tiering costs authoring effort — someone must decide which tier a lesson belongs in, and getting that wrong buries a lesson in a representation too weak to hold it. **Tier 3 must remain a genuine escape hatch, not a grudging fallback.** The classifier that assigns a lesson to a tier is itself new machinery with no prior art, and it is the second-highest-risk item in this milestone after rebase.

### Suggested addition to the decomposition

- **Tier classifier + tiered delta store** — the representation decision and its storage. Precedes the delta grammar work.
- **Learning budget + consolidation policy** — the token ceiling, demotion, and umbrella merge.
- Reprioritize **inspection/control** (`gaia skill deltas`, readable diffs, a visible count) far earlier. Reviewers of Hermes consistently single out that its learning is *legible* — a file you can open and diff — as what makes the feature feel real rather than claimed. Legibility is product surface, not tooling polish.

comments.body:
Adding a plainer summary, since the original write-up led with the mechanism instead of the impact.

**What happens:** you tell the agent to call `triage_inbox`, and it calls `pre_scan_inbox` instead.

**Why that's expensive:** the email quality benchmark works by sending exactly that instruction. It now scores 0 on every metric — not because classification got worse, but because it never receives the tool output it grades. The email quality gate is effectively switched off while this stands.

**Cause:** PR #2661 roughly doubled the pre-scan section of the system prompt, which outweighs a direct instruction naming the other tool.

## Triage

- **P0, blocks #2661 and #2662.** Neither should merge until this is resolved — merging removes the quality gate for everyone.
- Everything else in the wave-2 batch (#2655, #2656, #2657, #2658, #2659, #2660) is unaffected.
- Cheap to reproduce: one benchmark run, ~10 min. Check `tools_called` in the scorecard — that field is the signal, not the accuracy number.

## Suggested fix order

1. **Unblock first (small):** trim or rebalance the pre-scan prompt section so an explicitly named tool wins. This is the minimum to get #2661 mergeable and the benchmark scoring again.
2. **Then decide the real question (needs a call):** what *should* a plain "triage my inbox" do? `pre_scan_inbox` is the better answer for a user — it's the fast card. If that's the intent, the benchmark should be measuring that path rather than forcing the raw classifier, and `triage_inbox`'s docstring is right to steer away from it. That makes this partly a benchmark design bug, not only a prompt bug.
3. **Pin it:** a regression test on the routing decision. This failed silently — the only symptom was a full benchmark scoring 0.0, hours after the change landed.

The trap to avoid is fixing step 1 by editing the harness prompt or the docstring so they agree. That restores a green number tonight and leaves the gate just as liable to flip on the next prompt edit.

Re-prioritised **P0 → P2**, and here's my judgment on the design question, since it changes what this issue is actually about.

**This is primarily a benchmark design bug, not a prompt bug.** Two reasons.

**1. The product behaviour is arguably correct.** `triage_inbox`'s docstring has said since 2026-07-27 that it is *not* the tool for "triage my inbox" and that `pre_scan_inbox` should be used instead. `pre_scan_inbox` is the fast card the TUI actually renders. So a user asking to triage their inbox getting `pre_scan_inbox` is the intended design working. Nobody types "call `triage_inbox`" — only the harness does.

**2. The more serious problem underneath: the benchmark measures a path users don't take.**

- `pre_scan_inbox_impl` calls `triage_inbox_impl` with `classifier=None` — heuristic only. Messages the heuristic isn't confident about land in `needs_review`.
- The benchmark forces `triage_inbox`, which *does* get a classifier wired (`agent.py:1355`), so those same unconfident messages get resolved by the LLM.

So for exactly the hard cases, the benchmark records an LLM-resolved answer while the user gets "needs review". The 0.717 `category_accuracy` describes the heuristic+LLM path, and the card users look at is heuristic-only. Those are different numbers for different code.

There is already corroboration: `personal_recall` measured **0.182 with zero variance across three runs**. Zero spread means it's decided deterministically — the heuristic path — while the same runs scored 0.717 overall on the LLM-assisted path. Two paths, two very different quality levels, and only one of them is what a user sees. That's tracked separately as #2667 and is the same root observation as #2633.

## Revised severity

P2 is right. No user-facing impact — this only fires on an explicit by-name tool directive, which only the harness issues. It is measurement infrastructure, not product behaviour.

I'd also soften what I said earlier about it blocking #2661: it doesn't break anything for users. Merging #2661 leaves the email benchmark unable to score until the harness is reconciled — a real cost, since regressions would go undetected, but a tooling tradeoff to accept deliberately rather than a hard gate.

## Suggested direction (revised)

1. **Point the benchmark at the path users actually use.** Score `pre_scan_inbox`'s envelope rather than forcing the raw classifier. This measures what ships, and incidentally makes the harness robust to prompt changes instead of dependent on winning a tug-of-war with a docstring.
2. If per-message classifications are still wanted for scoring granularity, get them from a direct `triage_inbox_impl` call in the harness rather than by asking the agent in prose to pick a tool. A benchmark should not depend on the model's tool-routing decision to measure classification quality — that couples two unrelated things, which is what produced this.
3. Only if 1 and 2 are rejected: rebalance the pre-scan prompt section so an explicitly named tool wins.

Either way the earlier warning stands — don't reconcile the harness prompt and the docstring by editing one to agree with the other. That restores a green number and leaves the coupling in place.

**On `main@abb8ddea` this is no longer deterministic — it behaves as a coin flip, and it looks scale-sensitive.** That matters for anyone verifying a fix: a small run can pass while the real run silently fails.

Also worth linking — **this issue is very likely the unfound root cause in #2776**, which reports the benchmark's classifier "provably never fires" and states the suppression point was never located. Neither issue currently references the other.

<details>
<summary>🔍 Technical details</summary>

Measured today, `Gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF`, `--ctx-size 32768`, freshly regenerated 307-message corpus:

| Run | `--limit` | Tool called | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 25 | `triage_inbox` | PASS — `category_accuracy` 0.80, `within_one_bucket` 0.92, `llm_classified_count` 23/25, ~44.8k triage tokens |
| B | 307 | `pre_scan_inbox` | FAIL — `total_emails: 0` |
| C | 307 | `check_mailbox_access` → `setup_mailbox_access` | ERRORED — `AgentConsole has no request_user_input_blocking` |
| D | 307 | `pre_scan_inbox` | FAIL — `total_emails: 0` |
| E | 307, SLM on | `pre_scan_inbox` | FAIL — `total_emails: 0` |

So 3 of 4 full-corpus attempts rerouted, while the 25-message run honoured the directive. This issue's original table measured 2/2 deterministic at a pinned commit; that no longer holds. One plausible reading is that a larger requested batch makes the docstring's "raw per-message classifier, not for triage" framing read as more applicable — but that is a hypothesis, not something these five runs establish.

Run C is a separate failure mode also worth noting: the agent went looking for mailbox setup and hit a missing console method, in a context where no human can answer a prompt.

The acceptance criterion here — "a regression test pins the routing decision so a future prompt edit cannot silently flip it" — should probably pin it at more than one `--limit`, given the above.

For #3095's purposes we worked around this by driving the bulk triage path directly rather than through the agent loop, which removes the model's tool choice entirely. That is a measurement workaround, not a fix, and deliberately doesn't touch either side of the contradiction this issue says to resolve deliberately.
</details>
